paper_title: Strike a Chord! Modal Kinetic Typography

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We introduce modal kinetic typography, which animates a vector glyph to express a semantic concept while keeping it legible. Our key idea is to build motion from the glyph's natural vibration modes. Specifically, a finite-element eigenproblem assembled from the vector outline yields the glyph's softest modes, for the whole letter and for each of its parts, allowing it to bend. The problem's zero-energy solutions, i.e., rigid translations and rotations, are applied in closed form to each part, allowing parts to also move as blocks. To animate the glyph, a frozen video diffusion model supervises only the modes' amplitudes and phases. Our modal approach addresses two weaknesses of prior work. Free-form point optimization under video score distillation (SDS) moves each point and frame independently along noisy gradients, tearing the outline and causing jitter. In contrast, our modes are smooth along the outline and driven by a few whole-cycle harmonics, which restricts these gradients to smooth, seamlessly looping motion. On the other hand, structured alternatives rely on skeletons or keypoints from category-specific priors, whereas our modes come from the glyph itself; the only prior is a list naming each letter's moving parts, generated once for the whole alphabet by a language model. In modal kinetic typography, shape and motion are disentangled by construction: a single base outline is sculpted toward the concept, and the modal drive cannot alter it, so a letter can also be animated without being reshaped. Our method produces more articulated and smoother motion than Dynamic Typography and AniClipart at comparable or better concept alignment, with less glyph tearing than Dynamic Typography, and is preferred by human raters, including in a frozen-shape setting where motion alone must carry the concept. Our results were also preferred over Astra (GPT-6) by human raters.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Kinetic typography, text that moves, is used to convey tone, emphasis, and narrative. In practice, it is almost always authored by hand, keyframe by keyframe, even with dedicated tools for animating expressive text (Lee et al., 2002). Generative models have recently started to automate the creative process, first by reshaping letter toward concept and leaving it static, then animating it under video prior (Iluz et al., 2023; Tanveer et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2025; Park et al., 2024). The main difficulty with automation is that the motion must satisfy three demands, two of which pull against each other. Specifically, motion should be expressive: the animation of word should evoke its meaning, so that reader feels the snake in snake and the energy for corresponding prompt that may say jump, for example. Yet the glyph must remain legible: deforming glyph too freely could make it stop being letter. In addition, the motion must carry meaning of its own rather than ride on the shape. In the limit where the glyph may not be reshaped at all, the action is the only element left to express the concept, which is referred to as the frozen-shape setting (see 4). Recent work on Dynamic Typography (Liu et al., 2025) optimizes pixels or vertices directly against generative prior, where single representation performs the two jobs: the very same boundary points must move to sculpt the shape and to animate it. Shape and motion then compete for the same degrees of freedom, and the deformation that serves one is spent at the expense of the other, which is why free-form optimization struggles to embed motion cleanly. At the other end of the spectrum, methods that impose structure, such as detected keypoints or per-group homographies, borrow it from category-specific priors (e.g., human skeletons) and generalize poorly (Wu et al., 2025; Levy et al., 2026). These two families of methods thus struggle for the same underlying reason, the representation: what method allows to move. Underneath it lies second difficulty. The 1 Figure 1: Modal Kinetic Typography: Vibration modes of shape decide how it can move. letters vibration modes are computed from the glyph itself. Three whole-letter modes are drawn here for visual representation. The glyph is separately deformed toward the prompted concept. Animating few modes brings the letter to life while keeping it legible, with frozen video diffusion model supplying the only learning signal for their amplitudes and phases. Shown examples include: as bird beating its wings, as cat flicking its tail, an unsculpted (i.e., motion-only animation without reshaping) raising one arm. With each part of the letter carrying its own modes, the motion stays in the part the caption names, e.g., the tail swings while the bowl stays still. The outline bends smoothly rather than tearing, retaining letter legibility. Glyphs animate in Acrobat. video prior speaks through score distillation (SDS), whose gradients are noisy from step to step, and whatever the representation leaves free, that noise is free to move: when each point and frame can move independently, the outline tears and the motion jitters as result. In this work, we address both difficulties by changing the representation. Our key idea is to build motion from glyphs natural vibration modes. Viewed as thin elastic sheet, glyph outline has small repertoire of ways it bends most easily, given by the eigenmodes of its elasticity problem, which have long been used in graphics as subspace for deformation (Pentland & Williams, 1989; Barbiˇc & James, 2005). The softest of these eigenmodes span whole strokes and follow letters geometry, bending it smoothly rather than creasing it, e.g., opens and closes like pair of wings, swings its tail out from the bowl, and spreads its arms. Only the first few modes are useful: stiffer modes bend the outline over ever shorter lengths until they crease it with legibility compromised. Figure 1 shows three whole-letter modes for each example. Restricting motion to this basis serves two goals at once: (a) natural motion, since the letter moves only in the ways it bends most easily, and (b) legibility, since the stiffer modes that would crease the outline are excluded. Bending, however, is not the whole repertoire. The same eigenproblem has three zero-energy solutions: rigid translation in and y, plus rotation. When applied to whole letter, these would only shift or turn it, but when confined to part, they are exactly what limb needs, letting the part move as block while the joint absorbs the difference. We therefore write these three modes in closed form for each part, with parts taken from list generated once for the whole alphabet (3.2.2): the letters mechanics decide how part bends, and the list decides only where one part ends and the next begins. frozen text-to-video model then only has to supervise the modes amplitudes and phases over time (see purple arrow in Figure 1), problem with few dozen degrees of freedom rather than the thousands in free-form point optimization. We address the noise in SDS gradients by pairing the modal basis above with periodic drive, which expresses each modes coefficient over time as sum of few whole-cycle sinusoids. When every point in every frame has its own parameters, this noise reaches the motion in two ways: in space, neighbouring points are pushed apart and the outline tears; in time, point jumps between 2 frames and the loop jitters. Our modes suppress tearing: each is smooth field over the outline, so that neighbouring points move together, except across part joints, where an edge-length term penalizes stretching. At the same time, the drive suppresses jitter, where one set of sinusoid parameters shapes the whole loop, leaving no per-frame freedom for noise to occupy. SDS can therefore move the animation only along directions that are smooth along the outline and repeat over the loop, and the same loss that produces jitter under free per-frame drive yields smooth motion here (5, Appendix A.8). Our contributions can be summarized as follows: modal motion basis computed from glyphs outline in vector form: finite-element eigensolve over the glyphs interior gives the softest ways the whole letter and each of its parts bend, and closed-form rigid modes let each part move as block. The layers are orthogonalized, so parts move as blocks rather than being bent into place, and the basis displaces the outline itself, so every frame remains resolution-independent vector path. Smooth, looping motion intrinsic to the representation, not imposed by dedicated loss: periodic drive that expresses each modes coefficient as few whole-cycle sinusoids shared by all frames. Under the same SDS loss that makes the motion jitter when each frames coefficients are free, it yields smooth motion that loops seamlessly. Shape-motion disentanglement by construction: shape and motion live in separate representations, so they do not compete for the same degrees of freedom. Motion cannot alter the base outline, and letter can be animated without being reshaped.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Semantic and kinetic typography: Word-as-Image (Iluz et al., 2023) deforms vector outline toward concept under an image diffusion prior while regularizing legibility. DS-Fusion (Tanveer et al., 2023) blends glyph and concept in raster space via discriminator-guided latent diffusion model. VitaGlyph (Feng et al., 2026) transforms only the part of character that carries the concept, while MetaDesigner (He et al., 2025) coordinates language-model agents for glyph and texture. All four produce static results. Among animated approaches, Differentiable Variable Fonts (Parikh et al., 2026) make variable fonts design axes differentiable, enabling gradient-based editing and physics-based text animation, but stay within the variants the typeface defines. KineTy (Park et al., 2024) trains video diffusion model on kinetic-typography templates and outputs raster video, so its motion comes from templates rather than from the letter. Closest to our setting, Dynamic Typography (Liu et al., 2025) animates vector letters under video diffusion prior by predicting perframe control-point displacements with neural displacement field, so its motion lives in highdimensional, per-frame parameterization. Our work shares the vector and prior-guided setting, but replaces free-vertex motion with glyph-derived modal basis. Score distillation and structured motion: Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) (Poole et al., 2023) distills pretrained diffusion model into the parameters of differentiable renderer. Like prior vector animation methods (Gal et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025), we apply its video form through differentiable vector rasterizer (Li et al., 2020). When applied to per-frame vertex displacements, however, video SDS tends to tear outlines and jitter, so prior work stabilizes it by reducing the degrees of freedom through borrowed structures. AniClipart (Wu et al., 2025) moves keypoints from pretrained detector with category templates under an as-rigid-as-possible deformation. Articulated Kinematics Distillation (Li et al., 2025) distills motion onto skeleton, while Animus3D (Sun et al., 2025) and Sketch2Motion (Rai & Sharma, 2026) use score distillation to animate 3D assets, with the latter through an inferred skeleton. APAP (Yoo et al., 2024) deforms mesh through user handles under image SDS. LiveSVG (Levy et al., 2026) abandons distillation altogether, citing noisy gradients, and instead fits the SVG to video sampled from an image-to-video model with per-group homographies. We observe that tearing and jitter stem largely from what is optimized, hence we change the latter while keeping distillation. Specifically, the spatial basis comes from glyphs own vibration modes rather than rig, detected keypoints, or sampled video, and periodic drive shared by all frames yields smooth motion where free per-frame drive under the same loss would lead to jitter (5). Modal analysis and reduced deformable models: Using natural vibration modes as motion subspace is classical in graphics (Pentland & Williams, 1989; Barbiˇc & James, 2005), where 3 Figure 2: Pipeline of Modal Kinetic Typography: The letter is partitioned into articulation parts from fixed per-alphabet table (Appendix A.9). Each part contributes three rigid modes, written in closed form, and its two softest localized eigenmodes, alongside one whole-letter mode, so the basis Φ is the letters own. An analytic integer-harmonic drive supplies the coefficients αm(t); with Φ they give the displacement u(t), which rides on the sculpted template and is rendered differentiably. Sculpting joins only at step 250, since shape that satisfies the prior early may conflict with the demand that drives the motion. The frozen video prior sets how much of each mode is played, never what the modes are. The basis is solved once on the source glyph and never recomputed. Open padlocks mark the two optimized groups, the stylization MLP and the drives Amk, φr. few low-frequency modes span the deformations shape most easily undergoes. Modal warping (Choi & Ko, 2005) keeps such subspace valid under large rotations, Hauser et al. (2003) drive constrained deformation interactively within it, and localized variants confine modes to region, learned from examples (Neumann et al., 2013) or solved on the geometry as Localized Manifold Harmonics (Melzi et al., 2018). When geometry is unknown, projections of an objects vibration modes can instead be recovered from the temporal spectra of optical flow in video and used to simulate its response to new forces (Davis et al., 2015), and Generative Image Dynamics (Li et al., 2024) predicts such spectral motion from single image with diffusion model. However, both methods operate on raster pixels and derive motion from video, whereas in our work, glyphs vector outline gives us its geometry, so we solve for its modes directly to displace the outline. Reduced subspaces have also been used to control motion, e.g., optimal control (Barbiˇc et al., 2009), spacetime constraints (Hildebrandt et al., 2012), rest-shape actuation (Coros et al., 2012), and locomotion along bodys natural modes for legged characters (Kry et al., 2009; Nunes et al., 2012) and soft bodies (Benchekroun et al., 2024), with periodic oscillation long an animation primitive (Kass & Anderson, 2008). These control methods integrate motion from equations of motion or search for it against hand-specified objective. In contrast, we prescribe the temporal coefficients analytically and let frozen video prior supervise only their amplitudes and phases, so the motion is named in words rather than designed. On the basis itself, we confine modes to parts from list generated once per alphabet, add closed-form rigid modes per part, and orthogonalize the layers, so parts bending does not repeat what its rigid motion already expresses.

sections.title: 3 METHOD
sections.content: Given vector letter glyph and concept caption, we produce looping animation of the sculpted glyph, deforming its outline over time. Every output frame is deformed path, so the result is resolution-independent vector graphics. Two groups of parameters are optimized and they stay separate throughout. The first sculpts the glyph outline toward the concept. The second group sets only how that outline moves over the loop, through handful of coefficients shared by every frame. Neither can do the others work. Figure 2 shows the full sequence and illustrates which loss controls which aspect of the pipeline. 3.1 SHAPE SCULPT: GENERATING THE BASE SHAPE The glyphs shape is deformed toward the concept using the same machinery as Dynamic Typography (Liu et al., 2025). small network offsets the outline control points under video SDS through 4 differentiable rasterizer, with perceptual and conformal anchors preserving the source letter. We, however, differ in two ways. First, motion is established before sculpting begins (3.2.5), so shape optimization occurs on an already moving glyph, design set through empirical tests. Motion therefore acts as soft constraint so that edits that disrupt the learned articulation are discouraged. Second, we sculpt single template rather than per-frame geometry. Dynamic Typography can encode part of the concept in frame-specific offsets, which lets the form drift from frame to frame. Our modal drive animates one base outline, requiring the concept to reside fully in the base shape itself.

sections.title: 3.2 MOTION: A BASIS FROM THE GLYPH’S OWN MECHANICS
sections.content: 3.2.1 From glyph to motion basis mode is shape the outline takes when the glyph flexes in way its own geometry is soft to move. We compute them at two levels, the whole letter and individual parts. Modes should act on large regions rather than fine boundary detail, so we use coarse boundary, 48 uniformly spaced points, smoothed with periodic Gaussian. Its interior is filled with constrained Delaunay quality mesh of vertices RN 2 and triangles . Modes solved on this mesh are interpolated back to the full-resolution glyph outline. Assembling linear (P1) element matrices over , where the strain is constant within each element, yields the global plane-stress stiffness matrix and the lumped mass matrix (Appendix A.5). Here is the Hessian of the elastic energy at rest, while accounts for the amount of material that must be accelerated. The interior mesh is scaffolding and it only serves to assemble and . From and we then obtain the shapes vibration modes ϕ R2N , one displacement per vertex, by solving the generalized eigenproblem Kϕ = λ ϕ. (1) The first three eigenvalues are zero and represent rigid translation in and and rotation, as they store no strain energy. They are discarded from the whole-letter layer only. Rigid motion is kept per part. Each part receives its own three closed-form rigid modes, translation in and and rotation about the parts centroid, so limb can pivot without bending (3.2.2 defines the parts, 3.2.3 assembles the layers). Among the remaining modes we keep the softest few. Since λ = ϕKϕ/ϕM ϕ is elastic energy per unit of mass-weighted motion, small λ gives the most motion for the least deformation, which means large, smooth bends and sways. Stiffer modes bend the outline over ever shorter lengths and crease it, so they are dropped. Doubling the number kept per part buys no additional articulation (see the four-eigenmodes ablation, Table 2). The whole-letter layer of the reported basis keeps only the single softest mode, as it behaved most consistently across letters and typefaces in our runs, and widening this layer is left to future work. 3.2.2 Localized modes for parts Global modes move the whole letter together. part that articulates on its own needs modes confined to its region. Following Localized Manifold Harmonics (Melzi et al., 2018), we tie every point outside region to its rest position with stiff spring, (2) (cid:0)K + µ diag(1 /r)(cid:1) ϕ = λ ϕ, so the softest modes have nowhere cheap to move but inside r. The mesh, and are shared across regions, only the mask changes per solve. The penalty scales with the stiffness itself (µ = 10 times the mean diagonal of K). Where the part table defines joint band, the hard indicator is replaced by 1 wr (wr [0, 1]) where wr=1 inside the part and wr=0 outside, with smooth transition across the band, so limb can pivot about the joint rather than tear across it. Since µ is finite, confinement is soft, so mode can extend slightly beyond its region. Defining regions: Cutting the medial axis at its branch points was the obvious choice. However it returns single region on unbranched letters like C, I, and O, so no part can move against another. We instead define the parts once per alphabet: language model names each letters moving parts and places one seed per part. This part table is shared by every glyph, typeface and caption, and solves the issue of unbranched letters. At run time seeds snap to the medial axis, the axis is partitioned by growing outward from them, and each boundary point takes the label of its nearest axis point. The parts are identical on every run. This approach captures geometrical intuition which skeleton cannot, e.g., an is one pen-stroke but moves as two parts, an upright and base . 3.2.3 Hierarchical basis The basis has two layers: global layer holding the single softest whole-letter mode (3.2.1), and part layer holding each parts three rigid modes and two softest localized eigenmodes (3.2.2). letter of two, three or four parts therefore carries 11, 16 or 21 modes. The rigid modes are written in closed form rather than solved for, because with the rest of 5 the letter pinned the localized solver returns swing mixed with bending rather than clean pivot. The whole-letter rigid modes are not kept to discourage the model from prioritizing global motion. Since the parts cover the whole letter, moving it requires every parts rigid modes to agree, keeping the option but not making it short-cut. Orthogonalization keeps the modes separate: each mode is projected off the span of all modes before it. Rigid modes are ordered first, therefore the eigenmodes lose the swing the rigid modes already express and carry only the bending pivot cannot. This does not change which deformations are reachable, but without it over 80% of an eigenmodes energy on average repeats earlier modes, mostly its parts rigid motion, and the optimizer tends to bend parts into place instead of pivoting them. Two eigenmodes are kept per part, and doubling that only doubles the drive spent on eigenmodes without adding motion (Table 2, energy split in Appendix A.7). The whole basis is solved once on the source glyph, before any sculpting, and held fixed for the run (Appendix A.5), so the motion stays the letters own even as the outline moves toward the concept. 3.2.4 Motion model and periodic drive Let {Φm} be the assembled basis, all layers stacked as columns. The vertex displacement field is u(t) = (cid:88) αm(t) Φm. (3) Here Φm is the displacement pattern of mode over the outline, and αm(t) is scalar saying how much of that pattern is applied at time t. Its magnitude sets how far the outline moves along the mode, and its sign sets the direction. Each frame is the base outline plus u(t), with sampled at 16 evenly spaced points over one loop, so animating the letter amounts to choosing the curves αm(t). Learning each coefficient freely at every frame leaves nothing tying consecutive frames together, and the animation jitters  (Table 2)  . We instead write each coefficient as sum of integer harmonics with soft amplitude clamp, αm(t) = amax tanh (cid:16) 1 amax (cid:80)H k=1 Amk sin(2πk + φr(m)) (cid:17) , [0, 1). (4) Here amax is fixed bound shared by all modes; tanh softly clamps each coefficient to it. Animating with vibration modes and periodic oscillation has precedent in graphics (Pentland & Williams, 1989; Kass & Anderson, 2008; Kry et al., 2009; Nunes et al., 2012; Benchekroun et al., 2024). We aim for looping animations typical of kinetic typography, so the frequencies are fixed to whole cycles of the clip, = 1, . . . , with H=3; the fundamental itself is fixed (Appendix A.3). The sum is so the number of harmonics does not change the motions magnitude. Every normalized by mode of part shares one phase φr(m), its rigid modes and eigenmodes alike, and the whole-letter mode has phase of its own. This keeps the model simple, with single timing per part. What is learned is the relative phase between parts, which is the gait. The amplitudes Amk are learned, one per mode and harmonic. letter of three parts carries 16 modes, so 48 amplitudes and four phases, 52 numbers for the entire animation. Smoothness then follows by construction, with every coefficient sum of few sinusoids shared by all frames. There is no per-frame freedom for jitter to occupy, and each frames gradient informs every parameter rather than only its own (Appendix A.8). Three harmonics per mode and phase per part still leave wide range, from single sway to parts moving at different rates and in counterpoint. 3.2.5 Rendering, objective, and schedules The deformed paths are rasterized with DiffVG (Li et al., 2020), and frozen text-to-video diffusion model supplies gradients through video SDS. Two anchors based on Dynamic Typography (Liu et al., 2025), perceptual and conformal, hold legibility to the source glyph, and an edge-length term guards the part joints. Only the drives amplitudes and phases φ and the shape networks weights are optimized, never vertex trajectories. The drive starts first and sculpting joins at step 250 (3.1). Schedules are given in Appendix A.5.

sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: We evaluate single-letter animation in two settings, against two published baselines and (as reference point rather than baseline) Astra (GPT-6), closed-source system that authors SVGs directly. In the full task method receives letter and caption and must both reshape the glyph toward the concept and animate it, the setting Dynamic Typography (Liu et al., 2025) addresses. In the frozen-shape setting, the sculpting stage is switched off and the method may only animate the glyph, which is where AniClipart (Wu et al., 2025) is directly comparable. Astra shares neither methods 6 Figure 3: Glyphs animated by their resonance: Each row shows the input glyph followed by animation frames at fixed scale and position, beginning with the frame closest to the input. Motion combines the glyphs finite-element vibration modes, preserving smoothness and legibility. Shown are an breakdancer and strutting rooster. In the frozen-shape setting (last row), the unsculpted jiggles like jelly while retaining its original shape. Table 1: Quantitative comparison and user study in the Full task and Frozen shape settings. The last two columns report user-study rankings: first, second, and third place receive 2, 1, and 0 points, respectively. The visuals question is omitted for Frozen shape. Method Global Artic. Jerk Dead Temp. Stretch Conc. & Motion Visuals Dynamic Typography Astra (Full task) Ours (Full task) AniClipart Astra (Frozen shape) Ours (Frozen shape) 7.23 9.26 6.11 9.14 2.49 7.72 6.28 2.67 0.6% 0.950 12.40 0.25 49.1% 0.976 0.84 1.1% 0.966 9.24 5.22 1.58 0.3% 0.981 2.03 0.55 13.1% 0.998 10.83 0.92 1.6% 0. 9.05 1.47 3.32 1.24 1.11 2.03 18.23 19.08 19.54 18.67 18.35 18.86 14% 12% 27% 19% 1% 43% 0.89 0.79 1.32 1.17 0.34 1.48 0.82 0.90 1.28 we the For video diffusion model machinery: in both settings it receives our caption with the letter and typeface to apply it to, and answers in one shot. Each test case is letter, typeface and caption naming subject and its action, and produces sixteen-frame animation. We use language model to generate 100 cases per setting with random letters, over twelve typefaces. The two published baselines are evaluated at their default setting. Training Details: use ModelScope text-to-video-ms-1.7b (Wang et al., 2023), the same as published baselines, on single 24 GB GPU. Results are reported after 1000 optimization steps, of which the first 250 are motion only. The basis composition and the learning-rate schedules are given in Appendix A.5. Metrics: Global measures the glyphs overall movement and rotation and Articulated the remaining deformation, both as percentages of glyph size. Jerk is the third time-derivative of position over mean speed, and Dead time its counterweight, the share of samples whose acceleration is negligible. Stretch is our tearing measure. Temporal consistency (Wu et al., 2025) and Concept , an X-CLIP textvideo score (Liu et al., 2025), come from the two baselines. Details in Appendix A.10. These metrics should not be interpreted in isolation since jerk, temporal consistency and stretch are all flattered by clip that does not move, and concept similarity can be won by drawing with no letter in it. The last column therefore asks for two properties at once. Moves & legible (M & L) is the share whose articulated motion is at least half stroke width and whose form still reads as its letter in most frames. Beyond small motion, our margin there grows as the bar rises (Appendix A.11). Quantitative Comparison: Against Dynamic Typography, we use similar motion budget but favor articulated deformation over rigid translation. Our stretch is less than half theirs and lower in 95% of cases, while concept similarity, temporal consistency, and motion smoothness are higher. 7 Figure 4: Comparison with Dynamic Typography and Astra. The left-most column of each block is the input glyph, the prompt sits above, and the frames span the clip. Our motion stays within the letters structure. The toe lifts while the boot shaft stays upright, and the limbs swing while the holds its crossing. Dynamic Typography either barely moves or deforms the glyph heavily to move at all, and Astra draws clean icon that keeps little of the letter. Against AniClipart, we roughly double articulation while translating the glyph less, from lowdimensional parameterization in both cases. AniClipart uses category-specific control directions from pretrained detector, ours are the glyphs own vibration modes. It leads on temporal consistency and stretch, partly due to its as-rigid-as-possible objective and low-motion cases. Restricting to pairs where both methods move, our articulation still leads (13.44 vs. 8.52). Astra leads several geometric and temporal metrics, but largely by construction. Its rigid parts and analytic keyframe interpolation suppress jitter and tearing. This comes at the cost of glyph identity, as it redraws the subject rather than deforming the letter. In the frozen-shape setting, where redrawing is disallowed, its articulation collapses. Its high dead time reflects two failure modes: 44% of its ink never moves, and even across the half of the outline that moves most, 32% of samples carry no acceleration. This is the signature of constant-velocity interpolation between keyframes which reads as less realistic. User study: Each study contains 10 cases, answered by 44 participants on the full task and 39 on the frozen-shape task. For each case, participants rank the three clips, scored 2, 1, and 0 points and averaged in Table 1s last two columns (Appendix A.4 gives the full protocol). The full task asks which clip moves best and which has the better visuals while keeping the letters identity. Frozen shape asks only about motion. For the full task, five cases are representative Dynamic Typography examples and five are sampled from twenty cases where both Dynamic Typography and ours achieve strong concept alignment, all regenerated by the three methods on the same letter, typeface and caption. Frozen-shape cases are sampled from twenty where both AniClipart and ours exhibit strong motion. These criteria favor the baselines by including only cases where they have strong outputs. Ours leads on both full-task questions and on frozen-shape motion. Qualitative Comparison: Our animations alone are in Figure 3. Figure 4 sets the full-task ones beside Dynamic Typography and Astra, Figure 5 against AniClipart and Astra on frozen shape. Against Dynamic Typography our motion is more articulated and smoother, and it is localized where the caption asks for it rather than spread over the whole glyph. Against AniClipart it is again more articulated, and it reads as the action rather than as pose being nudged. Against Astra the difference is what the motion belongs to. Ours deforms the letter it was given and stays that letter, while Astra redraws the subject. In the frozen-shape setting, where it may not redraw, it struggles to produce motion at all. The captions own effect on the motion is shown in Appendix A.2.

sections.title: 5 ABLATIONS
sections.content: Free per-frame drive. Each modes coefficient is learned independently at every frame, in place of the harmonic drive of 3.2.4, with the basis and the loss unchanged. The animation jitters: jerk more than triples at the median and is worse in all 20 pairs, and temporal consistency falls. As an alternative we also tried an MLP α = net(t), zero-meaned to maintain looping. It collapsed to stillness, so we report the free table here and leave more learnable α(t) to future work. Global modes only. Every mode is made whole-letter eigenmode, keeping the mode count. Removing the part layer takes localization and per-part rigid motion together. Since the whole-letter 8 Figure 5: Comparison with AniClipart and Astra on the frozen-shape task. All three animate the same given outline, with no sculpting on any side. Driving the glyphs own modes gives fuller and more realistic articulation: the undulates along its length and the rocks on its uprights. AniCliparts keypoint rig, whose control directions are the same for any clipart, holds the letters closer to their rest pose, and Astra mostly declines to move the outline it is handed. sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION, LIMITATIONS, AND FUTURE WORK
sections.content: We present modal kinetic typography, which builds letters motion from its natural vibration modes and per-part rigid modes, with frozen video diffusion prior supervising only their amplitudes and phases. This yields smooth motion at less cost to legibility than free-form optimization and enables letter to move without being reshaped. Since the smoothness comes from the representation rather than dedicated loss, the modal approach should carry over to other SDS-driven dynamic content. Our representation still has limits (Appendix A.12). To start, single outline cannot change topology or turn in depth, hence glass cannot shatter, nor can flame flicker away. The drive is periodic by construction, excluding actions that end somewhere other than the start. More importantly, our results depend on how well the letter and typeface suit the concept. In particular, parts come from list fixed per letter rather than per concept, so when the subjects anatomy does not match the letters parts, limb may be forced to move with its neighbour or be split across two parts. Separately, part that does have its own region may still drift when the caption asks it to stay put, such as the base of hammer, since the supervision cues motion more strongly than its absence. Finally, our part list covers the uppercase Latin alphabet only, and we evaluate single letters rather than words. Future work could add non-periodicity to the drive, explicit constraints for stationary parts, and support for other scripts and words, and automatically choose letters to best suit prompt.

sections.title: A APPENDIX
sections.content: A.1 ABLATIONS, QUALITATIVELY Figure 6: Ablations, qualitatively. Each row compares the full model with an ablation using the same letter, caption, seed, and mode count. Top: The free per-frame drive jitters between consecutive weightlifter frames. Middle: Whole-letter modes move little beyond the hammocks rail tops. Bottom: Without orthogonalization the bird is dragged rather than pivoted. A.2 THE CAPTION CONTROLS THE MOTION As the video prior acts only through modal coefficients, the caption controls how the modes are played rather than what they are. Figure 7 holds the letter and its typeface fixed and varies only the action. On K, raises his sword and swings his sword give the same visual with distinct motions, where Dynamic Typography (Liu et al., 2025) produces nearly the same action for both. Figure 7: One glyph, two captions for the same subject, all else fixed. Ours raises the sword in one and sweeps it down in the other, while Dynamic Typography (Liu et al., 2025) moves similarly for both. A.3 SPEED IS KNOB Because the drive uses harmonics of one fundamental, action speed is set by single value rather than learned. Multiplying all harmonics by plays the basis times per clip. Figure 8 shows {0.5, 1, 2} with everything else fixed: the lizard takes half, one, or two strides in the same Integer preserves seamless number of frames. The action is unchanged; only its rate varies. looping because every harmonic completes an integer number of cycles, so =0.5 breaks the loop. 12 Figure 8: Effect of base frequency. A.4 USER STUDY DETAILS Participants were given the following brief, then shown one case per page. The brief describes the task as defined by prior work, Dynamic Typography (Liu et al., 2025). Both that method and ours deform the input outline, hence the briefs requirement applies to them equally. Kinetic typography aims to reshape letter toward prompted concept and animate it with natural, temporally coherent, and semantically faithful motion, while the result stays recognizable as the letter. Both shape and motion should arise from the letters own structure, its strokes, parts, mass, and symmetry, rather than being pasted on, with motion that is smooth, plausible, and timed to convey the described action most naturally. Each page shows one prompt, the original letter, and the animations of it. Please watch every animation fully, then rank them for each question. Give each rank to exactly one animation. The two questions are: Q1: Which animation exhibits the most realistic and smoothest motion? Q2: Which animation has most realistic and high quality visuals while keeping the letters base identity? Q1 is reported as Motion in Table 1 and Q2 as Visuals; in the frozen-shape setting, where no method may change the glyph, only Q1 is asked. Figure 9 shows page as participants saw it. A.5 IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS Operators use Poisson ratio ν=0.3 and unit Youngs modulus, which scales the eigenvalues uniformly without changing mode shapes or their ranking. Eq. 1 is solved sparsely for the smallest eigenpairs. The basis is solved once, on the source glyph before any sculpting, and is held fixed for the whole run rather than being recomputed as the outline changes. Motion learning rates warm up for 200 steps to 0.30 for amplitudes and 0.03 for phases, then cosine-decay to half. The shape learning rate warms up for 300 steps, peaks at 1.1 102, and log-linearly decays to 4.4 103. Every run uses seed 0. Each frame is rasterized differentiably at 320 320, and clip is 16 frames. Score distillation uses classifier-free guidance at scale 30, with the diffusion timestep drawn uniformly from [50, 949] of the models 1000-step schedule at every step and the usual (1 αt) weighting on the gradient. The amplitude bound of Eq. 4 is amax = 20.7 px on that canvas, shared by every mode; modes are normalized to unit RMS displacement, so the bound means the same thing for each of them. Of the loss terms in 3.2.5, the perceptual and conformal anchors are weighted at 2000 each and the edge-length term at 100. 13 Figure 9: One page of the study. The prompt, the base letter, and the three methods animations in randomized order, labelled only A, and C. Participants watched each clip in full and then answered the two questions below the page, giving each rank to exactly one animation. A.6 VISUAL EXAMPLE OF MODES Figure 10 drives two modes of one letter by hand, without the video prior. Figure 10: The two kinds of eigenmode, driven by hand. V: above, the softest whole-letter mode; below, mode confined to its left diagonal. A.7 SPREAD OF ENERGY ACROSS THE BASIS Table 3: Mode for mode the eigenmodes carry little more than the closed-form rigid modes, and the optimizer drives both about equally hard. Layer Modes Energy Per mode Peak coefficient Whole letter Per part, rigid (closed form) Per part, localized eigenmodes 1 3 each 2 each 8.2% 53.0% 38.8% 8.2% 17.7% 19.4% 7.72 6.156.60 6.527. A.8 WHAT THE DRIVE CAN AND CANNOT EXPRESS Score distillation may ask for anything, but only the part of its request that the basis can express reaches the animation. In time the basis is three whole-cycle harmonics per mode. Table 4 gives the resulting motion spectrum, beside the free per-frame drive of 5, which changes only this. Above the third harmonic the full model carries 0.0004 of its moving power against the free tables 0.186, higher in all 20 cases, which is what the jerk column reports. 14 Table 4: What reaches the animation. Share of moving power per temporal harmonic of the realized motion, median over the 20 ablation cases. The free per-frame drive keeps the same spatial basis and changes only the temporal parameterization. Drive k= k=2 k=3 > 3 Full model (whole-cycle harmonics) Free per-frame drive 0.598 0.495 0.120 0. 0.081 0.055 0.0004 0.186 A.9 THE ARTICULATION-PART TABLE We show the table rather than describe it. Figure 11 gives the realized partition for five letters, in two of the papers twelve typefaces, chosen to be of very different construction. The table has 26 entries, or 75 named parts, produced once for the alphabet. Every case, concept and typeface in the paper reuses it unchanged. Figure 11: The articulation-part table, and its transfer across typefaces. Five letters with their parts coloured, in two of the twelve typefaces we animate. A.10 METRICS AND LETTER FIDELITY Definitions of the measured columns of Table 1, in the order the table reports them, together with the letter-match measure its last column is built on, followed by the shape measures and the percase evidence behind them. One measure is taken from each published baseline so numbers stay comparable with the work they come from; the rest are ours. Motion: reported as two separate numbers, because two quite different things both count as movement. letter can travel, sliding and turning across the frame while its form stays exactly as it was, and it can articulate, with one part moving relative to the rest, which is what an action such as leg swinging or wing beating looks like. So for each frame we ask how much of the movement is explained by carrying the letter around as one rigid piece. That share is Global and everything left over is Articulated , so the two never count the same movement twice. glyph that merely flies across the canvas scores high on the first and near zero on the second. Concretely, every method logs the same outline points in each of the frames, so clip is table of positions rather than video and the movement is read straight off it, instead of being estimated from the pixels, which is unreliable inside solid silhouette. We take the letters rest shape to be the average of its frames. For each frame we then find the single rotation and translation that best carries that rest shape onto it, in the least-squares sense, and apply it. Whatever this transform accounts for is the letter moving as one piece, the distance still separating the two shapes afterwards is movement no rigid motion can explain. Averaged over all points and frames, that leftover is Articulated, and subtracting it from the total movement away from the rest shape leaves Global. Both are divided by the letters radius, the typical distance from its centre out to its outline, so the numbers read as percentages of letter size and compare across typefaces and canvas scales. Before the split we also trim the trajectory to the temporal frequencies carrying most of its movement, which sets little of the frame-to-frame flicker aside. 15 Jerk : the third time-derivative of the control-point positions, divided by mean speed. Dividing by speed makes it scale-free, so method is not penalised for moving further. Dead time : the share of trajectory samples whose acceleration is negligible next to what single loop-frequency harmonic of the same speed would have. The test is on acceleration alone, so coasting at constant velocity counts as dead exactly as standing still does. Jerk is minimised by motion that barely happens, so dead time is its counterweight. Temporal consistency : the mean cosine similarity between consecutive-frame image features, as reported by Wu et al. (2025). While designed to measure smooth motion, it is maximised by glyph that does not move. Stretch : maxi ℓi/ℓ over boundary edges relative to rest length, our tearing measure. Rest is the frame-mean shape, which for zero-mean drive is the template itself. Edges shorter than tenth of the median rest length are excluded, since dividing by them detects pinching rather than tearing, and no edge is ever formed between two contours. Concept : X-CLIP score between the clip and the caption (Liu et al., 2025). Shuffling frames alters the score by < 2%, so we treat it strictly as concept-similarity measure and leave motion to the user study. Reads as letter: the share of frames that still read as the intended letter. Each frames ink is binarized, cropped and scaled into fixed box with aspect ratio preserved, then matched by intersection over union against all 26 uppercase letters rendered in bank of typefaces, keeping the best typeface per letter, so the question is whether the form reads as some rather than one specific A. The cases own typeface family is held out, so method that deforms that outline earns no credit for having started from it; holding it out costs our score five points, Dynamic Typographys six and Astras one. On clean glyphs set in held-out typeface the matcher recovers the right letter 88% of the time. Moves & legible asks for pair of properties at once. Every column above can be won without solving the task. Jerk, temporal consistency and stretch are all flattered by clip that does not move, and concept similarity by drawing with no letter in it or even no motion. This metric thus is the share of cases whose articulated motion is at least half stroke width and whose form still reads as its letter in most frames. The bar is set in stroke widths because that is the scale of the thing being moved, the median stroke width of the evaluation typefaces is 14.7% of glyph size, so the bar is 7.4%. Beyond small motion our lead grows as the bar rises, and Figure 12 sweeps it. A.11 EXPRESSIVENESS AGAINST LEGIBILITY The tradeoff our representation is designed to weaken appears clearly across cases. As motion increases, legibility tends to fall, especially for the baselines. The correlation is ρ = 0.30 for Dynamic Typography and 0.40 for Astra, compared with 0.21 for ours. Figure 12 shows the same pattern directly. At modest motion, ours and Dynamic Typography are similar (50% vs. 52% legible), but the gap widens as more movement is required. At half stroke width, 27% of our cases both move that much and remain legible, compared with 14% and 12% for the baselines. In the frozen-shape setting, the same point is 43% for ours, versus 19% and 1%. The two panels fall away for different reasons. On the full task the baselines trade the letter for motion: among the clips that clear the bar, only 44% of Dynamic Typographys and 19% of Astras still read as their letter, against 47% of ours. In the frozen-shape setting AniClipart instead rarely reaches that much motion at all, clearing the bar in 32% of cases against our 70%, while among the clips that do clear it legibility is alike (57% against 61%). All curves begin below 100% because the matcher, with the cases own family held out, already misses the clean unanimated glyph in the harder display and script faces. That floor is where the frozen-shape curves start together; on the full task Astra starts lower still, since it redraws the letter rather than deforming it. Either way, our glyph-derived basis buys motion without spending the letter. A.12 LIMITATIONS What the representation cannot express. Every frame is displacement field on one base outline, so the letter deforms without changing topology. Actions that break apart or dissipate, such as fire, are outside the method (Figure 13). For the same reason turn in depth is unavailable, since there is no far side of the glyph to bring into view and no occlusion to reorder. Rotation within the 16 Figure 12: Motion against legibility. The dashed line is the bar used for the moves & legible column of Table 1. plane is available through each parts rigid rotation mode, but it is the linearized one, which carries points along the tangent rather than the arc, so part driven far around it lengthens rather than turns. The animation is likewise closed loop by construction, since the drive is built from whole-cycle harmonics. We choose this for seamless repetition, at the cost of actions meant to end somewhere other than where they began; nothing in the basis requires it, and non-returning component in the drive would lift the restriction. Figure 13: Three captions that ask for something outside the representation. Top: the glass is asked to shatter, but one closed outline cannot separate, so it wobbles whole. Middle: the flame is asked to flicker, which would need tongues that detach and die away, so the wick only leans. Bottom: the vane is asked to turn, but the in-plane rigid mode is linearized, so the arm rocks and returns rather than coming round. Eight frames spanning the clip in each row. Sensitivity to the letter and the typeface. The available motion is the letters own, so the outcome depends on how glyphs geometry suits the concept, and the same concept on the same letter animates differently in different typeface. On asked for pair of steel scissors opening wide and snapping shut, heavy face keeps thick blades that part little (articulation 8.0) while light one gives thin blades that open wide (articulation 17.0), both plausible scissors with different motion (Figure 15). The partition does not adapt to the concept. The number of parts is itself controllable, and the part table can name as many as letter needs. What is fixed is that the decomposition is decided once per letter, while the decomposition that suits the animation may depend on the concept. An could be pair of scissors or starfish: the scissors divide naturally into two blades, whereas the starfish needs finer division for each arm to move on its own. Figure 16 shows the cost of too coarse division, merging the starfishs four parts into halves and then into one taking most of its articulation 17 away. Future work could choose the number of parts and their assignment from the target concept rather than from the letter alone. Stationary parts and motion suppression. While our motion representation can assign different amplitudes to individual modes and parts, we observe that parts expected to remain stationary may still exhibit unintended motion. For example, an signpost swings its sign but carries the post along with it, and hammer swings its head but carries its base, where both supports should stay near still (Figure 14). In principle, the optimization could suppress such motion by learning sufficiently small amplitudes for the corresponding components, suggesting that this behavior is not necessarily limitation of the representation itself. Rather, the optimization may not always provide sufficiently strong signal to distinguish between parts that should actively move and those that should remain fixed. One possible explanation is that the motion supervision provides stronger cues for the desired movement than for the absence of movement in stationary regions. Incorporating explicit stationary constraints or stronger spatial guidance could help address such cases. Figure 14: Parts the caption holds fixed still move. The signposts post moves 0.81 times as much as the sign it carries, and the hammers base 0.96 times as much as the head that swings, where both should be near zero. Figure 15: The same letter and caption in two typefaces. Nothing differs but the face the is set in, and the seed is the same. The heavier face keeps thick blades that part little, the lighter one gives thin blades that open wide. Figure 16: How finely the glyph is divided decides how much of the motion is articulation. Same letter, caption, typeface and seed; only the partition changes. With the part tables four parts each arm moves by its own amount, which is what the caption asks for (16.8% of glyph size, rigid share 0.21). Split into top and bottom half, the two arms in each half can only move together (8.7%, 0.35), and as one region the letter can only lean as whole (3.4%, 0.67).
